Traditional playing is close to percussion, using a rhythm of accented downstrokes and paired upstrokes that answers the zapateado steps. A beginner can first get to know the five-course arrangement — single strings at each side and three double courses between — and also the modern four-course double tuning GG CC EE AA. Its range lies mainly in the upper middle register, and its tone sits between the guitar and the mandolin, with the guitar's warm body and the mandolin's bright liveliness. The way the strings resonate gives a warm, full tone, and in fast plucking it produces a light, active, continuous stream of notes. Compared with the classical guitar the jarana is sharper and brighter; compared with the banjo it is softer and warmer. These qualities make it especially suited to impassioned dance music, and it fully expresses the warmth and energy of Mexican traditional music.

The jarana (jarana jarocha) is a fretted chordophone from southern Veracruz in Mexico, Hornbostel–Sachs 321.322-5, and belongs to the family descended from the Spanish Baroque guitar. Its body is narrower than a guitar's and is traditionally carved and hollowed from a single block of wood before the soundboard and fingerboard are fitted; it usually has eight strings in five courses, single at the outside and double in the middle. Playing uses accented downstrokes and paired upstrokes to make a rhythm close to percussion, answering the zapateado steps. It is usually played in ensemble with the arpa jarocha (Veracruz folk harp) and the guitarra de son (a four-string lead guitar) and others, for the rhythms of folk music.
